newsitem.title: GERMANY: German army morale soars with peacekeeping mission.
newsitem.headline: German army morale soars with peacekeeping mission.

text.p: Morale in the German army has soared in the last year because of the Bundeswehr's historic peacekeeping mission in former Yugoslavia, the country's top military officer said.

Inspector General Hartmut Bagger told a group of newspaper editors on Tuesday night in this village south of Bonn that motivation had surged since Germany's post-war ban on foreign operations outside NATO countries was lifted by parliament.
"We have seen a tremendous boost in motivation in the Bundeswehr," Bagger said in a speech at the Federal Academy for Security Policy think tank.
"Although we were structurally not prepared for such a mission in former Yugoslavia, the soldiers have proven themselves."
Bagger said the 4,000 German army troops who spent a year in Croatia and Bosnia on the IFOR mission that ended in December had brought back a wealth of experience.

Another 3,300 German troops are now based in Bosnia and taking part in the follow-up SFOR mission. Their deployment in December marked the first time in post-war history that Germany sent combat troops abroad.

"The peacekeeping mission has brought us so many positive effects," he said. "The willingness of the soldiers to help has generated so much pride, not just in the armed forces, but also in the public and in the parliament."

One barometer of that surge in morale is the enlistment rate, Bagger said. It climbed 28 percent in the last three years and eight percent last year as more conscripts opted for military service than the alternative civilian service.
The number of young people joining the army for their compulsory 10-month service plunged in the early 1990s.
"We're now facing the opposite problem of having so many recruits that we are having trouble finding adequate assignments for all the qualified people," he said.
Because of the excesses of World War Two there had long been a strong anti-military sentiment in Germany, which kept its armed forces on a decidedly short leash.
It declined to make its army available for any duties outside NATO and even then kept out of countries that felt the full force of Hitler's Wehrmacht.

Bagger said these restrictions had taken its toll on morale, which hit an all-time low during the Gulf War when Germany declined to send any forces to the U.N.-backed mission to oust Saddam Hussein from Iraq.

"The Gulf War was a trauma for us," said Bagger. "We had the highest level of draft dodgers ever. But that trauma prompted a discussion that led to the successful mission in former Yugoslavia. It all went astonishing fast for me."
